1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.name: Sicilian Defence: Old Sicilian
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.background: One of Black's three main replies to 2.Nf3, with 2...d6 and 2...e6. Lines beginning 2...Nc6 that do not transpose into lines of 2...d6 have their own ECO codes, B30–B39; the most important among them are the Rossolimo, Kalashnikov, Sveshnikov and Accelerated Dragon.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: The principled move: White trades the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn to open lines for every piece. Black keeps a d- and an e-pawn against White's single central pawn, White gets open lines for every piece, and the game turns open and sharp.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.background: Its earliest recorded game is Bird against Horwitz in 1851. The Nyezhmetdinov–Rossolimo Attack is named for Nicolas Rossolimo, who first played it in 1948, and Rashid Nezhmetdinov, who played it in 1956. It is very popular at the highest levels: Fabiano Caruana played it in games 1, 3 and 5 of the World Championship match against Magnus Carlsen.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards d4 and e5, with the aim of taking it and doubling Black's pawns. White accepts giving up the bishop for the knight and avoids the heavy theory of the open Sicilian, playing instead for a structural edge in a slower, strategic game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and waits, leaving the choice between opening the centre and a slower, closed set-up for later. The price of that flexibility is that Black can occupy e5 with a pawn, which makes d4 hard to play and leaves White with a quiet game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Portsmouth Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to pull Black's c-pawn away, so that White can build a big centre with open lines. Black's extra pawn is paid for and the game stays level, so the gambit is sound, but a pawn is a lot to give for equality.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will help control the centre and make it harder for White to build a pawn centre, and the king gets a safe home. Black accepts the threat of doubled pawns for a solid game, with counterplay on the queenside or from the d4 outpost.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Brooklyn Retreat Defence
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.strategy: Undoes 2...Nc6 for nothing: Black has lost two tempi, and White's knight and bishop are developed while Black's army is still at home. The bishop on b5 achieves little, but White can take the centre at once and without risk.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5.strategy: Sidesteps the bishop and avoids doubled pawns, but puts the knight on the rim, where it no longer guards d4 and e5 and can be harassed by the b-pawn. White gets a free hand in the centre against a badly placed piece.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O.strategy: Brings the king to safety and the rook towards the centre. White keeps the exchange on c6 in reserve and plays it when it can double Black's pawns, so Black has to decide how to meet that threat while finishing development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.Bxc6.strategy: Cashes in the bishop at once to wreck Black's pawn structure: whichever way Black recaptures, the c-pawns are doubled. In return Black gets the bishop pair, so White has to show that the structural damage counts in the long, manoeuvring game that follows.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.c3.strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre, but e4 stays without a defender and the pawn takes the c3 square from the knight. White builds slowly while Black completes the fianchetto, and the exchange on c6 stays in reserve for a better moment.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop watches the long diagonal towards the centre and the queenside, and Black can castle once the knight is out. It also makes White's plan of a broad pawn centre harder to carry out.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat: the knight attacks the e4 pawn, which nothing protects, so White has to spend a move on it. Black gets the knight out first and keeps the fianchetto of the bishop in reserve.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O d6.strategy: Guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop, but it is slow here. With the f8-bishop and the king's knight still at home, Black meets 5.d4 without the pieces to challenge the centre, and White gets the freer game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.R.strategy: Supports the e-pawn, so that Black's knight development does not win time against it, and keeps two plans alive: a broad pawn centre and a space-gaining advance of the e-pawn. White stays flexible and commits to a patient, strategic game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.strategy: Prepares a pawn centre at once, but leaves e4 without a defender: Black's knight can attack it immediately, so White has to deal with that before the plan goes on.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.B.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight at once to double Black's pawns on the c-file. Black gets the bishop pair and the g7-bishop keeps its long diagonal, so White has to make the damaged pawn structure count in a slow game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.strategy: Develops with a threat: the knight attacks the unprotected e4 pawn, so White's centre plan comes with a price, either a pawn offer or a detour to protect e4. The most natural way to punish the missing rook on e1.

Takes the centre with a pawn and makes it hard to build one of White's own, but blocks the bishop on g7 and leaves d5 as a hole. Unlike the natural knight move it does not hit e4, which gives White time to organise.
A solid set-up that guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop, but it does not challenge e4, so White gets the full pawn centre at once. Black has to be ready to meet the central advance with exchanges.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation, Gufeld Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.strategy: A gambit: White offers the d-pawn, which Black's two pawns and knight attack, to open the centre and trade off Black's central pawns. The compensation is open lines for the pieces and the pressure of the bishop on b5, at the cost of material.

Supports e4 with a pawn and opens the diagonal of the c1-bishop. Black's pawn on e5 shuts in the g7-bishop, so White can build up patiently, improve the pieces and keep the exchange on c6 in reserve instead of forcing matters in the centre.

Defends e4 with the rook and keeps a central break in reserve until it can be supported. A flexible waiting move, though it ties the rook to the e-pawn and does not by itself challenge Black's compact set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation, Totsky Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.strategy: Solves the problem of e4 at once, since the queen defends it along the fourth rank, and adds a second attacker to the knight on c6 behind the bishop. White keeps the pressure on the knight while the pawn centre stays intact.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation, Lutikov Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.c.strategy: A gambit: with e4 still unprotected, White opens the centre at once and leaves both d4 and e4 under attack. The compensation is piece activity and the threat of taking on c6, and it is risky, since White has to make up the lost material.

Defends the attacked e4 pawn with a developing move, so the queen stays at home and the pawn centre stays intact. White has already played c3 for a broad centre, and Black has to castle and decide how to meet the central advance.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.R.strategy: Takes space in the centre and stops White from advancing the e-pawn, but blocks the bishop on g7 and leaves a hole on d5. Black gets a solid, closed structure, while White can pick the moment to take on c6.

Develops the knight with a natural attack on e4, which the rook defends, and finishes the fianchetto set-up without blocking the bishop. If White advances the e-pawn, the knight has a good square on d5; otherwise Black castles into a harmonious position.

Guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop: a solid, slightly passive set-up that keeps White's e-pawn from advancing easily. Black gives up the quick ...d5 break and accepts a little less space, but the position holds together.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.R.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Gurgenidze Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6 4.O-O Bg7 5.R.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to pull Black's c-pawn away from the centre, aiming at a broad pawn centre and open lines. It is an unusual wing gambit that costs a pawn for the sake of initiative and space, and Black can accept it calmly.

Supports e4 with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, a patient build-up against Black's blocked fianchetto. The pawn on e5 shuts in the g7-bishop, so White can improve the pieces without hurry and still choose when to take on c6.

Prepares the central break the earlier moves were heading for, but it still needs support, because Black's two pawns and the knight all bear on d4. The pawn also takes the c3 square from the knight. A logical plan that Black has time to prepare for.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5 4.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, San Francisco Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5 4.b4.strategy: Strikes at the displaced knight at once: the pawn attacks both the knight and the c5 pawn, offering a pawn to harass a piece that stands badly. The gambit costs material if Black simply takes it and defends calmly.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, because Black has moved the same knight twice and left it on the rim. Open lines favour the side with the better-placed pieces, and the exchange on d4 brings White's pieces out faster. A good, direct plan.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5 4.O-O.strategy: Castles at once while Black's knight stands offside on a5. Black needs time to bring it back into play, and meanwhile White keeps every central plan, d4 included, in hand.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Anti-Sveshnikov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Plants a pawn on e5 that guards d4, so White can no longer open the game with d4. Black gets space in the centre but leaves d5 as a hole, since neither the c5 nor the e5 pawn can cover it, and the game turns into a slow manoeuvring fight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Keeps the pawn structure healthy and opens the diagonal for the f8 bishop, with d5 covered. Black answers a central break or a bishop sortie with a flexible, sound set-up and heads for a normal Open Sicilian game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Holds e5 against a later e-pawn push and frees the c8 bishop, a compact set-up in familiar Sicilian territory. Black lets White choose between opening the centre at once and a quieter development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop on the long diagonal, where it presses on the centre and on the c3 knight from a distance. Black keeps the d-pawn at home, so ...d5 stays available in one move, and the game stays flexible.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4.strategy: Puts the bishop on its most active square, eyeing f7, where Black can no longer shield the diagonal with an e-pawn move. With the pawns on c5 and e5, neither covers d5, which stays a long-term outpost for White.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bb5.strategy: Targets the c6 knight, which holds e5 and covers d4, hoping to double Black's pawns. Black is not obliged to allow it: the knight can jump to d4, and the bishop's pressure often comes to little.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.d3.strategy: Guards e4 with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop, the quiet way to keep a closed centre. White gives up the pressure on f7 that the bishop on c4 brings, so Black develops freely.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7.strategy: A solid developing move that prepares castling and guards g5, so White's knight cannot jump there to double the attack on f7. Black keeps the structure intact and waits, accepting a modest game in which White controls d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8 bishop, leaving the bishop on f8 to come out when Black likes. The structure is compact, and Black accepts a modest game in which White controls d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a hit on e4, but 5.Ng5 puts a second attacker on f7, guarded only by the king. Black must find 5...d5 and still stands worse after 6.exd5 Nd4, so the natural-looking move hands White the initiative.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop. White gives up the idea of opening the centre and plays a slow, safe build-up, keeping the pressure on f7 and the control of d5 in the background.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.O.strategy: Gets the king to safety first and keeps the pawn support for e4 in reserve; the set-up is the same slow build-up in another order. The price is that White commits the king before knowing where Black will put the pieces.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.N.strategy: Occupies the hole on d5 at once and offers to swap the knight for the e7 bishop, which would give White both bishops. The cost is time: the same knight moves twice while Black develops, so the idea gains nothing lasting.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Anti-Sveshnikov Variation, with d6
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.strategy: Props up the e5 pawn with a pawn and opens the c8 bishop, giving Black a compact structure with no obvious target. Black accepts a slightly passive game in which White's pieces have more room and White holds the d5 square.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Anti-Sveshnikov Variation, with Nf6
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.strategy: Develops with a direct hit on e4, keeping the active ...d5 strike in mind instead of the slower pawn move. But the knight blocks the bishop's view of g5, so White can bring a knight there to double the pressure on f7, and Black has to be ready for it.
A waiting move that takes b5 away from the bishop and knight and prepares to chase the bishop with a pawn. It develops nothing and does not fight for d5, so White gets time to build up.

Clears the way for the f-pawn, so White can plan a kingside pawn break while the bishop on c4 and the knight on c3 keep d5 under control. The cost is that the knight blocks the c1 bishop for now, and the plan is slow.

Gets the king to safety and connects the rooks before committing the pieces. White keeps the bishop on its active diagonal and the control of d5, and plays a patient game in which Black has no obvious target.

Develops the last minor piece and keeps both castling sides open, with the bishop eyeing c5, which d6 guards solidly. It is sound but gives White no plan of its own, and Black has time to complete development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Anti-Sveshnikov Variation, Kharlov-Kramnik Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.background: Vladimir Kramnik played 6...Bg5 as a common alternative to 6...Nf6.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bc4 Be7 5.d.strategy: Reroutes the bishop to an active diagonal, where it controls f4 and keeps White from the natural f-pawn advance, and puts the d2 knight under pressure. Black avoids a passive game and challenges White's plan at once.
The natural developing move: it hits e4 and prepares to castle, leaving the c8 bishop free. Black keeps a solid structure and meets White's slow plans without committing to a counter-plan of its own.

Challenges the strong bishop at once. If White takes, the recapture with the f-pawn doubles Black's e-pawns but opens the f-file and controls d5; if White declines, the bishop sits actively and the pressure on f7 is gone.
